solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Go away, I hear, in Oxford? (4)

indicatorNotes.I hear: what you hear is a sound, so the letters come from how the word is said

blocks.note: 'shoo!' is what you say to send someone away

annotation.surface: Someone is told to clear off, perhaps by a snooty don in the university city.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford looks like the city, but an oxford is also a laced leather shoe.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the oxford is one style of lace-up footwear, named after the city.

entries.clue: Viking, say, casting copper base (5,5)

indicatorNotes.casting: casting metal melts it and reshapes it, so the letters are remade

annotation.surface: A Norse warrior is pictured casting a bronze stand in a forge.
annotation.walkthrough: Viking suggests a Norseman, but the Viking missions were NASA landers sent to Mars in the 1970s; 'say' warns that it is an example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Viking 1 and 2 were unmanned craft sent to explore Mars.

entries.clue: Unsettled arguments King dismissed (5)

indicatorNotes.dismissed: a dismissed person is sent away, so the letter leaves the word

blocks.note: R = Rex, king; it is removed

annotation.surface: Arguments rumble on after the king has been sent packing.
annotation.walkthrough: ROWING here rhymes with 'cowing', a British word for loud quarrels, not boating.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a bill: one not yet paid is still due.

entries.clue: Artist cuts press off about Pound (10)

indicatorNotes.off: something off has gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled
indicatorNotes.about: the jumbled letters go round the next piece

blocks.note: L = pound sterling (libra); it goes inside after the third letter

annotation.surface: An artist chops the printing press out of a project to do with Ezra Pound.
annotation.walkthrough: Capitalised Pound suggests the poet; it is the pound sign's L.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a woman who carves or models figures is one kind of artist.

entries.clue: Yellow bit of kit stylish nurse grabs (7)

indicatorNotes.bit of: a bit is a small piece, here the opening letter
indicatorNotes.grabs: whatever grabs something holds it inside

blocks.note: first letter of kit, held inside

annotation.surface: A smart nurse snatches up a piece of yellow equipment.
annotation.walkthrough: CHIC and EN together grab the K. Yellow here is cowardly, not a colour.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the slang sense: both words mean cowardly.

entries.clue: Old star left upset, tenor admitted (7)

indicatorNotes.admitted: someone admitted is let in, so the letter goes inside

blocks.note: upset = angry; it takes in the T

annotation.surface: A fading celebrity walks out in a huff after a tenor is let in.
annotation.walkthrough: Lillie Langtry was a Victorian stage actress and society beauty. 'Upset' reads as a mixing signal but is simply ANGRY.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Lillie Langtry was a famous actress of the 1880s, a star of long ago.

entries.clue: Icon in Carry On Matron originally (5)

indicatorNotes.originally: originally points to the start, the first letter

blocks.note: first letter of Matron, placed on after TOTE

annotation.surface: A symbol of the Carry On films: the 1972 comedy Carry On Matron.
annotation.walkthrough: The Carry On films were a long-running series of British slapstick comedies; here 'On' just places M after TOTE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a carved emblem revered as a symbol is an icon.

entries.clue: Duke who played Duke out of western (9)

indicatorNotes.out of: the letter is taken out of the word

blocks.note: the Duke of Wellington, victor of Waterloo

annotation.surface: An actor who played a duke has fallen out of a cowboy film.
annotation.walkthrough: The first Duke is Duke Ellington, the jazz bandleader who played piano; the second is Wellington.
annotation.definitionFit: A title used as a nickname: the jazz pianist Edward Ellington was known as Duke.

entries.clue: Very very fair (2-2)

annotation.walkthrough: Very very suggests excellent, yet the answer means only middling.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair in the sense of a fair result, neither good nor bad, is middling.

entries.clue: A force probing hacks’ ID badges (8)

blocks.note: hacks = nags, tired horses; they hold the rest
the Met is London's Metropolitan Police force

annotation.surface: The police are investigating journalists' press passes.
annotation.walkthrough: Hacks look like journalists but are horses; A and MET go inside them.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: badges pinned on to show who you are.

entries.clue: Am I not in a foreign type of film? (9)

indicatorNotes.foreign: foreign letters are strange ones, so they get rearranged

annotation.surface: A viewer asks whether this is a foreign-language picture they appear in.
annotation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder runs across five short words that read like a question, which is what hides it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genre: cartoons made from drawn or modelled frames are one kind of film.

entries.clue: Those a player lays down to score (5)

annotation.definition: Those a player lays down to score

blocks.note: not a footballer or musician but someone at a board game
the pieces are placed on the board, and each carries points

annotation.surface: A sportsman puts things down to rack up points.
annotation.walkthrough: The player suggests sport or music, but it is a Scrabble player laying letter tiles on the board.
annotation.definitionFit: In Scrabble or mah-jong the small pieces placed to score are tiles.

entries.clue: Winger mostly keen to hold line (5)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most but not all, so the last letter is lost
indicatorNotes.to hold: the shortened word holds the next piece inside

blocks.note: eager = keen; mostly drops its R, leaving EAGE
L = line, held inside after the third letter

annotation.surface: A wide player is desperate to keep to the touchline.
annotation.walkthrough: Winger reads as a football wide man but means anything with wings.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-style definition: any bird has wings, so a bird of prey is a winger.

entries.clue: Drug … take mine to get high (8)

indicatorNotes.to get high: getting high scrambles you, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: A dealer offers his own stash for a buzz.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is one long offer, so the break after 'Drug' is easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the anaesthetic also taken recreationally is one drug.

entries.clue: Head office? (10)

blocks.note: not a company's main site but the person at the top of a country
not a building but a post, the position someone holds

annotation.walkthrough: Head office suggests a company headquarters; it is the office, the post, held by the head.
annotation.definitionFit: The post held by a head of state is literally the head's office.

entries.clue: Official coach has no time for strain (7)

indicatorNotes.has no: the word goes without the letter

blocks.note: T = time, removed to leave RAIN

annotation.surface: A referee's trainer can't find a moment for an injured muscle.
annotation.walkthrough: Strain suggests an injury but means a musical phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical sense: a strain is a tune, and one repeated in a song is its chorus line.

entries.clue: Possibly save for trip or break (4,5)

annotation.surface: Maybe you put money aside for a journey or a holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trip or break' reads as a pair of holidays; break is the definition, meaning to go to pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that breaks up comes to pieces.

entries.clue: Hearty travelling around cape? (7)

indicatorNotes.travelling: letters on the move are rearranged
indicatorNotes.around: the rearranged letters go round the next piece

blocks.note: C = cape, as on maps; it goes after the second letter

annotation.surface: A hardy sailor rounds a headland.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a hearty is a sailor ('me hearties'), and one sailing round a cape is a yachter.
annotation.definitionFit: An &lit: read straight, a sailor rounding a headland describes someone out in a yacht.

entries.clue: Orchestrate an arrangement a cute lad plays (3,1,4)

annotation.surface: A handsome boy performs a musical arrangement he has orchestrated.
annotation.walkthrough: Orchestrate and arrangement pull towards music; together they mean to settle terms.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to broker an agreement is to strike a bargain.

entries.clue: Blunder in juggling? (5-2)

blocks.note: British slang for a botched job, a mess
a juggler keeps the balls in the air

annotation.walkthrough: A balls-up is British slang for a botched job; the question mark flags the literal second reading.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for a mess, and literally what a juggler keeps: the balls up in the air.

entries.clue: One enters before old lady gets award (7)

indicatorNotes.enters: to enter a place is to go inside it, so the letter goes inside the word

blocks.note: old lady = mother, mum; it takes in I

annotation.surface: Someone goes in ahead of an elderly woman, who wins a prize.
annotation.walkthrough: Old lady is slang for mother, not an elderly woman.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a prize or bonus paid out is an award.

entries.clue: Old lover cares for presents (7)

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner

annotation.surface: A former partner still looks after the gifts.
annotation.walkthrough: Presents is a verb, as in extending a hand, not gifts.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb sense: to hold out an offer or a hand to someone is to present it.

entries.clue: Transport proposal EU leader leads (7)

indicatorNotes.leader: a leader is at the front, here the first letter
indicatorNotes.leads: going first, it comes at the front

blocks.note: a motion is a proposal put to a meeting

annotation.surface: The head of the European Union fronts a plan on transport policy.
annotation.walkthrough: Transport is a strong feeling, as in transports of joy, not vehicles.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary sense: a transport is a rush of overwhelming feeling, as in transports of delight.

entries.clue: Cook cut slicing fruit and cheese (8)

indicatorNotes.cut: a word that is cut is trimmed short, so the cook loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.slicing: a knife slicing goes into the thing

blocks.note: a mango, split to take in the cook
CHEF, a cook, trimmed of its last letter

annotation.surface: A chef chops fruit and cheese for a platter.
annotation.walkthrough: Cook is a noun, the chef, not an instruction to cook.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Spanish sheep's-milk cheese from La Mancha.

entries.clue: Droll gripes making liberal mad primarily (5)

indicatorNotes.making: making one thing into another swaps the letter
indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily points to the first letter

blocks.note: first letter of mad, put in place of L

annotation.surface: Wry complaints that drive a Liberal politician wild.
annotation.walkthrough: The gripes are bellyaches, colic, not complaints; turning its L into M gives the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: drily amusing means funny.

entries.clue: Went out in old hat (5)

annotation.surface: Someone stepped outside wearing an ancient hat.
annotation.walkthrough: Old hat looks like a piece of headgear; it is the idiom for old-fashioned.
annotation.definitionFit: The word covers both senses: courting someone, and being behind the times.

entries.clue: Close to breakfast, ready to eat baloney (5)

indicatorNotes.Close to: the close of a word is its end, the last letter

blocks.note: ripe fruit is ready to eat

annotation.surface: Nearly breakfast time, and someone is ready to tuck into processed meat.
annotation.walkthrough: Tripe is both offal and nonsense, which is why the meaty surface is apt; baloney is itself a sausage.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the slang sense: both words mean nonsense, and both are also meats.

entries.clue: Spelling Rod, Welsh article failed ultimately (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, the last letter

annotation.surface: A Welshman called Rod could not spell 'article' in a test.
annotation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name; a spelling rod is one that casts spells.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-style definition: a rod for casting spells is what a wizard carries.

entries.clue: A large division warning of danger (5)

blocks.note: an arm is a branch or division of an organisation

annotation.surface: A big army division is told danger is coming.
annotation.walkthrough: Division suggests a sum or an army unit; here it is a branch, an arm of a larger body.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bell or siren sounded when danger threatens.

entries.clue: Faux leather at top coming off cap? (9)

indicatorNotes.at top: the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a cap is a limit, a limitation

annotation.surface: Fake leather peels off the top of a hat.
annotation.walkthrough: Faux leather reads as one phrase; faux alone is the definition, and cap means an upper limit.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowed French word: faux, meaning false, describes fake fur or fake pearls.

entries.clue: Reserve squad? (10)

blocks.note: reserve in its sense of aloofness, holding back
a unit of troops sent off on a separate task

annotation.walkthrough: Reserve squad reads as the second team; the two words are separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: The word covers both senses: emotional aloofness, and a military unit split off from the main force.

entries.clue: Refuse to believe study by unknown (4)

blocks.note: a den is a study, a private room

annotation.surface: Someone rejects research by an anonymous author.
annotation.walkthrough: Study looks like research but is a room.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to reject a claim as untrue.
